name: Projection and MIP Techniques
text:
# Projection and MIP Techniques

Also called: MIP (Maximum Intensity Projection)

## Overview
Projection and MIP Techniques are a family of [direct volume rendering](#1184-direct-volume-rendering.md) methods that generate 2D images by aggregating scalar values along viewing rays using operators other than the standard emission-absorption [compositing](#2436-compositing.md). They solve the problem of visualizing specific volumetric features—such as high-density bones, contrast-enhanced vessels, or low-density airways—by emphasizing extremal or cumulative values while suppressing intermediate background data. This family is distinct from [Compositing and Blending](2515-compositing-and-blending.md) because it discards opacity accumulation and depth cues in favor of order-independent aggregation (max, min, sum) or geometric approximation, and from [Volume Raycasting Output Generation](4277-volume-raycasting-output-generation.md) by focusing on these specific projection primitives rather than general output pipeline integration.

## Shared principles
All methods in this family share the fundamental structure of ray generation and traversal as defined in [Direct volume ray casting](19-direct-volume-ray-casting.md). For each pixel, a ray $r(t) = \mathbf{o} + t\mathbf{d}$ is intersected with the volume domain, and samples are taken along the ray segment. The core distinction lies in the aggregation function $A$ applied to the sampled scalar values $s_i$:
$$ A = \text{Aggregate}(s_0, s_1, \dots, s_{N-1}) $$
Common aggregators include:
- **Maximum:** $A = \max_i(s_i)$
- **Minimum:** $A = \min_i(s_i)$
- **Summation:** $A = \sum_i s_i \cdot \Delta t$ (line integral)

These methods are generally order-independent (except for summation where order does not matter, but the result is cumulative), allowing for flexible traversal orders and [early termination](#4675-early-termination.md) strategies. They inherently lose depth information, producing 2D projections that lack explicit spatial cues regarding the relative position of structures along the ray.

## Subtopics

### [Maximum Intensity Projection](902-maximum-intensity-projection.md)
[Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP)](#10702-maximum-intensity-projection-mip.md) projects the maximum scalar value encountered along each viewing ray. It sets itself apart from siblings by using the maximum aggregation operator, which highlights high-intensity structures like blood vessels or bone while suppressing lower-intensity tissue. It is chosen when the goal is to visualize high-contrast anatomical features without the occlusion effects of [alpha blending](#5750-alpha-blending.md). See [Maximum Intensity Projection](902-maximum-intensity-projection.md) for implementation details.

### [Projected Slabs Approximation](1449-projected-slabs-approximation.md)
[Projected Slabs Approximation](#1449-projected-slabs-approximation.md) accelerates perspective volume rendering by approximating the perspective view volume with a series of parallel projected slabs. It sets itself apart from scalar aggregation methods by providing a geometric approximation that enables the use of hardware optimized for parallel projection. It is chosen when interactive frame rates are required for perspective views on hardware lacking native perspective ray-casting support. See [Projected Slabs Approximation](1449-projected-slabs-approximation.md) for implementation details.

### [Forward Projection (aTx)](1492-forward-projection-atx.md)
[Forward Projection (aTx)](#1492-forward-projection-atx.md) computes the line integral of volume density along each ray, simulating X-ray attenuation. It sets itself apart by aggregating all encountered densities to provide a cumulative measure of material thickness, unlike MIP which only highlights the peak. It is chosen for generating synthetic radiographs or for visualizing the total mass of dense structures. See [Forward Projection (aTx)](1492-forward-projection-atx.md) for implementation details.

### [Minimum Intensity Projection](5299-minimum-intensity-projection.md)
[Minimum Intensity Projection](#5299-minimum-intensity-projection.md) (MinIP) projects the minimum scalar value along each viewing ray. It sets itself apart from MIP by selecting the lowest values, making it suitable for visualizing low-density structures such as airways or tumors in contrast-filled vessels. It is chosen when the target features have intensities lower than the surrounding background. See [Minimum Intensity Projection](5299-minimum-intensity-projection.md) for implementation details.

### [Projection](7205-projection.md)
Projection (Summation) visualizes the total accumulated intensity by summing voxel values along the ray. It sets itself apart from extremal projections (MIP/MinIP) by aggregating all data, creating a "total intensity" map. It is chosen for quantitative analysis of total density or when a simple orthographic projection is sufficient. See [Projection](7205-projection.md) for implementation details.

### [Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP)](10702-maximum-intensity-projection-mip.md)
This entry refers to the specific implementation variant of MIP often used in standard [raycasting pipelines](#8376-volume-raycasting-pipeline.md). It sets itself apart by emphasizing the order-independence and the specific handling of the accumulator initialization to $-\infty$. It is chosen for general-purpose high-intensity visualization. See [Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP)](10702-maximum-intensity-projection-mip.md) for implementation details.

### Perspective Approximation via Orthogonal Slices
An approximation for perspective volume rendering that uses view-orthogonal slices instead of concentric spherical shells, which are expensive to generate [S2]. The only difference from exact [ray casting](#6080-ray-casting.md) is that the distances of sample positions along a ray depend on the ray's orientation [S2]. Exact perspective ray casting produces associated sample positions forming concentric spherical shells, not planes. Generating these shells is expensive [S2].

### ProjectionVolumeStyle
A non-composable render style. An example image shows Bronchial tubes rendered with maximum intensity projection (MIP) [S3, unofficial].

## Background
The concept of Maximum Intensity Projection (MIP) originated in the early 1990s as a method to visualize contrast-enhanced vascular structures in CT angiography, allowing radiologists to see vessels without the clutter of surrounding tissue [S5, S11, S23, unofficial][S29, book][S30, S35, unofficial]. The term "MIP_Mode" appears in early [GPU raycasting](#6192-gpu-raycasting.md) implementations, such as those in the Visualization Library, where it was distinguished from other raycasting modes like Isosurface or [RaycastBrightnessControl](#6526-raycastbrightnesscontrol.md) [S1, unofficial]. The approximation of perspective projection using parallel slabs was explored to leverage hardware [acceleration](#18-acceleration.md) designed for orthographic views, addressing the performance bottleneck of generating spherical sample shells [S1, unofficial][S2]. Forward projection (aTx) is rooted in the physics of X-ray attenuation and computed tomography, where the line integral represents the projection data acquired by scanners [S1, unofficial]. Minimum Intensity Projection (MinIP) was developed as a complementary technique to MIP for visualizing low-density structures like airways in CT scans [S1, unofficial][S2].
